i: Break the ice
To do or say something that relieves tension or awkwardness, especially when meeting someone new.
He told a joke to break the ice at the start of the meeting.
Hit the books
To start studying seriously.
I have an exam tomorrow, so I need to hit the books tonight.
Piece of cake
Something very easy to do.
Don't worry about the test - it'll be a piece of cake.
Under the weather
Feeling slightly ill.
She stayed home today because she was feeling under the weather.
Once in a blue moon
Something that happens very rarely.
He visits his hometown once in a blue moon.
Cost an arm and a leg
To be very expensive.
That new phone cost an arm and a leg.
Hit the nail on the head
To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem.
You hit the nail on the head when you said we needed more practice.
Let the cat out of the bag
To reveal a secret by accident.
He let the cat out of the bag about the surprise party.
On the ball
Alert, competent, and quick to understand things.
She's really on the ball when it comes to deadlines.
Speak of the devil
Said when a person who was just mentioned suddenly appears.
Speak of the devil, here comes Sarah now.
Burn the midnight oil
To work or study late into the night.
He burned the midnight oil to finish his essay before the deadline.
Bite the bullet
To force yourself to do something unpleasant or difficult.
I finally bit the bullet and went to the dentist.
Call it a day
To stop working on something for the rest of the day.
We've done enough for now - let's call it a day.
Get the ball rolling
To start something or get a process moving.
Let's get the ball rolling on the group project this week.
Miss the boat
To miss an opportunity because you acted too slowly.
If you don't apply this week, you'll miss the boat.
On thin ice
In a risky or precarious situation, likely to face trouble.
He's on thin ice with his teacher after missing two assignments.
Pull yourself together
To calm down and behave normally after being upset.
Take a deep breath and pull yourself together before the interview.
Spill the beans
To reveal secret information.
Come on, spill the beans - what happened at the party?
Take it with a grain of salt
To not take something too seriously or literally.
He exaggerates a lot, so take his story with a grain of salt.
The ball is in your court
It's your turn to take action or make a decision.
I've done my part - the ball is in your court now.
Throw in the towel
To give up on something.
After three failed attempts, he finally threw in the towel.
Under your belt
Something you have already achieved or experienced.
With two years of experience under her belt, she felt ready for the promotion.
Cut corners
To do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often lowering quality.
They cut corners on the renovation and it shows.
Get cold feet
To become nervous or hesitant about doing something you had planned.
He got cold feet right before his speech.
Go the extra mile
To make a special effort to achieve something.
She always goes the extra mile to help her classmates.
Jump on the bandwagon
To join others in doing something popular.
Once one team started using the new app, everyone jumped on the bandwagon.
Keep an eye on
To watch or monitor something carefully.
Can you keep an eye on my bag while I get coffee?
Kill two birds with one stone
To achieve two things with a single action.
By walking to school, he kills two birds with one stone - exercise and saving money.
Lose track of time
To not notice how much time has passed.

Make a long story short
To summarise something briefly.
To make a long story short, we missed the flight.
On the same page
To agree with someone or understand a situation the same way.
Let's make sure we're on the same page before the presentation.
Out of the blue
Unexpectedly, without warning.
She called me out of the blue after years of silence.
Play it by ear
To decide how to act as a situation develops, without a fixed plan.
We don't have a set schedule - we're just playing it by ear.
Pull someone's leg
To joke with or tease someone.
Relax, I was just pulling your leg.
See eye to eye
To agree with someone.
The two of them finally saw eye to eye on the project plan.
Sit on the fence
To avoid making a decision or taking a side.
He kept sitting on the fence instead of picking a team.
Straight from the horse's mouth
Information heard directly from the person who knows the facts.
I heard it straight from the horse's mouth - she's transferring schools.
Take the plunge
To decide to do something you have been hesitant about.
He finally took the plunge and applied for the scholarship.
The best of both worlds
A situation combining the advantages of two different things.
Living near campus but close to the city gives her the best of both worlds.
Time flies
Time passes very quickly.
Time flies when you're having fun.
Blow off steam
To release built-up energy or anger.
He went for a run to blow off steam after the exam.
By the skin of your teeth
To narrowly succeed at something.
We caught the train by the skin of our teeth.
Come rain or shine
No matter what happens.
He jogs every morning, come rain or shine.
Cut to the chase
To get to the point without wasting time.
Let's cut to the chase - do we have a deal or not?
Down to earth
Sensible, practical, and modest.

Every cloud has a silver lining
Even bad situations have some positive aspect.
Losing that job was hard, but every cloud has a silver lining - I found a better one.
Give someone the benefit of the doubt
To believe someone's explanation without proof, trusting them.
I'll give him the benefit of the doubt this time.
Go back to the drawing board
To start planning something again because the previous attempt failed.
The design didn't work, so it's back to the drawing board.
Hang in there
To stay positive during a difficult situation.
I know exams are tough - just hang in there.
In the same boat

It's not rocket science
Something is not difficult to understand.
Just follow the instructions - it's not rocket science.
Keep your chin up
To stay positive despite difficulty.
Keep your chin up - the results will get better.
Let sleeping dogs lie
To avoid bringing up an old problem that could cause trouble.

No pain, no gain

Training every day is tough, but no pain, no gain.
Off the top of my head

Off the top of my head, I'd say the meeting is at 3pm.
Practice makes perfect
Doing something repeatedly improves your skill.

Put all your eggs in one basket
To risk everything on a single plan.

Ring a bell
To sound familiar.

Rule of thumb
A general, practical guideline, not an exact rule.
As a rule of thumb, arrive fifteen minutes early.
Sit tight
To wait patiently without doing anything yet.
Sit tight - the results will be posted soon.
Stick to your guns
To hold firmly to your position despite pressure to change.
She stuck to her guns even when others disagreed.
The tip of the iceberg
A small, visible part of a much larger problem or situation.
The delayed project is just the tip of the iceberg - there are bigger issues.
Water under the bridge
A past problem that is no longer important and has been forgotten.
We argued last year, but that's water under the bridge now.
Actions speak louder than words
What someone does matters more than what they say.

Add insult to injury
To make a bad situation even worse.

A blessing in disguise
Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good.

A dime a dozen

A drop in the ocean

The donation was generous, but it's a drop in the ocean compared to the total cost.
A leopard can't change its spots

A penny for your thoughts
A way of asking someone what they are thinking about.

A taste of your own medicine

Back to square one
Starting over again from the beginning.

Bark up the wrong tree

Beat around the bush
To avoid getting to the point of an issue.

Beggars can't be choosers
People with few options should accept what's available, without complaint.
It's not the flat I wanted, but beggars can't be choosers.
Bend over backwards
To make a great effort to help someone.
She bent over backwards to make sure the guests felt welcome.
Better late than never
It's better for something to happen late than not at all.
He finally replied to my email after three weeks - better late than never.
Bite off more than you can chew
To take on more responsibility than you can handle.

Bite your tongue
To stop yourself from saying something you want to say.
I had to bite my tongue when he took credit for my idea.
Break a leg
A way of wishing someone good luck, especially before a performance.
You'll do great tonight - break a leg!
Break the mould
To do something in a completely new way, different from what came before.

Bring home the bacon
To earn money to support a family.
Both parents work full-time to bring home the bacon.
Burn bridges
To destroy a relationship or opportunity so it can't be used again.

Burst someone's bubble
To spoil someone's excitement or illusion by telling them an unwelcome truth.

Butterflies in your stomach
A nervous, fluttery feeling before something important.

By the book
Strictly following the rules.

Can't judge a book by its cover

Caught red-handed

Chip on your shoulder
A lasting feeling of resentment, often from a past grievance.

Clear the air
To resolve a disagreement or remove tension between people.

Close but no cigar

Cross that bridge when you come to it
To deal with a problem only when it actually happens, not before.

Curiosity killed the cat
A warning that being too inquisitive can get you into trouble.

To be more lenient or less critical of someone.

Devil's advocate

Diamond in the rough

Draw a blank
To be unable to remember or think of anything.

Drive someone up the wall

Face the music
To accept the unpleasant consequences of your actions.

Fall from grace
To lose status, respect, or a good reputation.

Fit as a fiddle
In very good physical health.

Fish out of water
Someone who feels awkward or uncomfortable in an unfamiliar situation.

Flash in the pan
Something that seems promising or successful briefly, then fails to last.

Foot the bill
To pay for something, especially something expensive.
The company agreed to foot the bill for the training course.
From scratch
Starting from the very beginning, without using anything already made.

Get out of hand
To become uncontrollable.

Get the short end of the stick
To be treated unfairly compared to others in the same situation.

Get your act together
To organise yourself and start behaving more effectively.
You need to get your act together before the exams start.
Give someone the cold shoulder
To deliberately ignore or be unfriendly towards someone.

Go against the grain
To do something that goes against usual expectations or natural tendencies.
Speaking up in that meeting went against the grain for him.
Go cold turkey
To stop a habit suddenly and completely, rather than gradually.

Go down in flames
To fail spectacularly.
The plan went down in flames within the first week.
Go with the flow
To relax and accept things as they happen, rather than resisting.

Grasp at straws
To try desperate, unlikely solutions when in a difficult situation.

Hang by a thread
To be in a very precarious or uncertain situation.

Have a change of heart
To change your opinion or feelings about something.

Have bigger fish to fry
To have more important things to deal with.

Head over heels
Completely and intensely in love.

Hit the sack
To go to bed.
It's late - I'm going to hit the sack.
Hit the road
To leave or begin a journey.
We should hit the road before the traffic gets bad.
Hold your horses
Wait, slow down, or be patient.
Hold your horses - we haven't decided anything yet.
In hot water
In trouble.
He's in hot water with his manager after missing the meeting.
In the heat of the moment
Acting or speaking without thinking, due to strong emotion at the time.
She said something unkind in the heat of the moment and regretted it later.
In the nick of time
At the last possible moment, just before it's too late.
He caught the train in the nick of time.
It takes two to tango
A situation or disagreement involves both people involved, not just one.
Don't blame only him for the argument - it takes two to tango.
Jump the gun
To act before the right or appropriate time.
Let's not jump the gun and announce it before it's confirmed.
Keep your fingers crossed
To hope for good luck or a good outcome.
I'll keep my fingers crossed that the weather stays fine for the trip.
Kick the bucket
To die (informal, often used humorously).
The old washing machine finally kicked the bucket after ten years.
Kill the mood
To ruin a pleasant or enjoyable atmosphere.
His complaining really killed the mood at dinner.
Knock on wood
Said to avoid bad luck after mentioning something hopeful.
We haven't had any problems so far - knock on wood.
Know the ropes
To understand how to do a task or job well, through experience.
Ask Sarah - she's been here for years and knows the ropes.
Last straw
The final problem in a series that makes a situation unbearable.
The delayed train was the last straw after a difficult day.
Let bygones be bygones
To forget past disagreements and move forward.
They decided to let bygones be bygones and start over as friends.
Light at the end of the tunnel
A sign that a difficult situation is finally coming to an end.
After months of hard work, they could finally see light at the end of the tunnel.
Long shot
Something unlikely to succeed, but still possible.
Getting the last-minute tickets was a long shot, but it worked.
Lose your touch
To lose a skill or ability you once had.
He hasn't scored in weeks - has he lost his touch?
Make ends meet
To have just enough money to cover basic living costs.
With prices rising, it's getting harder to make ends meet.
Method to the madness
A logical reason behind what seems like strange or chaotic behaviour.
His desk looks chaotic, but there's a method to the madness.
Miss the mark
To fail to achieve the intended goal or result.
The advert missed the mark with younger audiences.
Music to my ears
News or information that is very pleasing to hear.
Hearing the project was approved was music to my ears.
Needle in a haystack
Something extremely difficult to find.
Finding that one file on the old server was like looking for a needle in a haystack.
Never say never
Don't rule something out completely, since things can change.
I said I'd never move abroad, but never say never.
Nip it in the bud
To stop a problem early, before it becomes worse.
The teacher nipped the disruption in the bud before it spread.
No news is good news

We haven't heard from them, but no news is good news.
Not my cup of tea
Not something you personally enjoy or prefer.
Horror films are really not my cup of tea.
On the fly
Doing something quickly, often without much preparation.
He wrote the speech on the fly just before the event.
On the house
Given free by a business, especially a bar or restaurant.
The waiter said our desserts were on the house.
Once bitten, twice shy
A bad experience makes you more cautious in future.
She won't lend him money again - once bitten, twice shy.
Out of the woods
Past the most difficult or dangerous part of a situation.

Over the moon
Extremely happy or delighted.
She was over the moon when she got the job offer.
Par for the course
What's typical or expected in a given situation.
Delays on this route are par for the course, unfortunately.
Piece of the pie
A share of something, especially profits or benefits.
Every partner wants a bigger piece of the pie.
Pull the plug
To stop or end a project or activity.

Pull the wool over someone's eyes
To deceive or trick someone.
He tried to pull the wool over our eyes, but we checked the facts.
Put your foot in your mouth

An offer to do something at a later time instead of now.
Can I take a rain check on dinner tonight? I'm exhausted.
Raining cats and dogs
Raining very heavily.
We stayed inside because it was raining cats and dogs.
Rock the boat
To do or say something that disturbs a stable situation.
Everyone was happy with the plan, so nobody wanted to rock the boat.
Run out of steam
To lose energy or enthusiasm for something.
The team ran out of steam in the final ten minutes of the match.
See the light
To finally understand or accept something after not doing so before.
After the warning, he finally saw the light and changed his approach.
Set in stone

Sit on the sidelines
To avoid getting involved in an activity or decision.

Spill the tea

The apple doesn't fall far from the tree

The last resort
The final option, used only when everything else has failed.

The whole nine yards

To act boldly without worrying about risk.

Tie the knot
To get married.

Tighten your belt

Turn a blind eye
To deliberately ignore something you know is wrong.

Turn the tables
To reverse a situation so that the disadvantaged side now has the advantage.

Under the radar
Without attracting attention.

Up in the air
Undecided or uncertain.
Our holiday plans are still up in the air.
Up to speed
Having the most current information about something.
Let me get you up to speed on what happened while you were away.
Walk on eggshells
To behave very cautiously to avoid upsetting someone.

Wear your heart on your sleeve
To openly show your emotions.
She's always worn her heart on her sleeve, even as a child.
When it rains it pours
Difficulties often seem to happen all at once.

When pigs fly

Wild goose chase

Wrap your head around something
To understand a difficult or confusing idea.

You can't enjoy two incompatible benefits at the same time.

Your guess is as good as mine

All ears
Ready and eager to listen.

Down in the dumps
Feeling sad or depressed.

Something that sounds simple but is actually difficult to do.

Get a grip
To take control of your emotions and calm down.

In a nutshell
Expressed briefly and simply.

On cloud nine
Extremely happy.

In both good times and bad times.
